newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Analyst views mixed on failed Swedish merger.
newsitem.headline: Analyst views mixed on failed Swedish merger.

text.p: A potential merger between two of Sweden's four big banks, S-E-Banken and Nordbanken, failed on Monday with no reason given but analysts said differences on pricing or staff could have sunk the deal.
After months of market speculation that helped fuel bank sector stocks, commercial bank S-E-Banken and state-controlled Nordbanken surprised the market by announcing talks were over.
"Nordbanken and Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken have discussed a possible merger. These discussions have been brought to an end without result," the banks' statement said.
Neither the banks nor the government, that controls the state's 59 percent stake of Nordbanken, gave a reason.

Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said government plans to sell out of the bank would continue and analysts suggested this could be to institutional shareholders or by repeating last year's successful share buyback scheme in a year or so.
Analysts listed a variety of reasons that could have blocked the merger.

Fiba analyst Jan Dworsky said up to 4,000 jobs would have been cut from a workforce of 16,000 if the merger went ahead - and the government was already battling a high unemployment hat was running at 8.7 percent in December.
"This is a very sensitive issue because the government is such a large shareholder," Dworsky told Reuters.
Another Stockholm based analyst, however, was adamant that staffing was not the reason the discussions broke down.
"It is said that S-E-Banken's owners could not agree on the state's price, that it was quite simply too expensive," the analyst said.
Banking analyst Abigail Leach from Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said the two banks possibly disagreed over how to handle their operations after a merger.
"I think that Nordbanken wanted to be more aggressive and close a large number of branch offices, something that S-E-Banken did not agree with," Leach told Reuters.
"I am rather glad that the merger did not go ahead. I like Nordbanken as an individual share."
One analyst said a disagreement about control of management after the merger could have contributed to the end of talks.
The banks' shares were not expected to lose out from the end of talks and quickly stabilised after an initial slump.
In afternoon trade Nordbanken was nine down at 226 crowns after hitting a low of 210 crowns and S-E-Banken down five at 67.50 crowns after a low of 67 crowns.

Analyst Robert Grant from C.S. First Boston was positive about Nordbanken's share and even expected S-E-Banken stock to hold up well even though the commercial bank was seen as the loser with the talks collapsing, actively seeking to expand.
Rumours about S-E-Banken seeking to merge with Handelsbanken last autumn bit the dust when Handelsbanken made a bid for mortgage bank Stadshypotek so this was seen as the second failed courtship.
Analysts said maybe S-E-Banken would look regionally, or to the insurance sector, or to Swedish banks Swedbank or Foreningsbanken for growth.

"On fundamentals Nordbanken still looks attractive in valuation terms and 240 to 250 crowns a share is certainly achievable although under a merger it could have been 270-280 crowns," Grant told Reuters.
"S-E-Banken's share price was held up by speculation of a merger but I think some of this speculation could continue and S-E-Banken shares could be supported at these levels."
($1=7.31 crowns)
